learning_objectives.label: Take a focused injury history (mechanism, onset, location, severity, associated symptoms)
Examine the injured wrist systematically and compare with an uninjured area
Choose imaging and interpret what its result does and does not exclude
Measure, choose and fit a wrist support, checking circulation and comfort

hints.text: Start by introducing yourself and asking what happened.
Examine more than one area: the sore part, the area next to it, and the uninjured side for comparison.
If an examination hurt, acknowledge it before you carry on.

interpretation: Difficulty: Guided. Coaching hints appear on their own as the encounter goes on.
Setting: Outpatient clinic room, quiet; noise level 25% at the end.
This scenario is experimental, not clinician-reviewed.

feedback.summary: No conversation transcript was recorded, so history-taking and communication could not be assessed. You examined the injured right wrist. However, you did not ask about the mechanism of injury (how exactly the patient fell). Correct. A fall on an outstretched hand with anatomical snuffbox tenderness makes a scaphoid fracture the key diagnosis to suspect and exclude.

next_steps: Complete the wrist examination: scaphoid tubercle tenderness and pain on axial thumb compression.
Request dedicated scaphoid-view radiographs; an initial X-ray can be normal.
If clinical suspicion remains despite normal X-rays: immobilise in a thumb spica splint and arrange repeat imaging or MRI.
Explain the plan and the risk of a missed scaphoid fracture (non-union, avascular necrosis) to the patient.
